issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
Walter is a 77-year-old married man who has spent most of his adult life working, and he still drives deliveries several days a week. He describes the assault as the moment his understanding of other people and of himself “just broke.” Late one afternoon, while making a routine drop-off, he was approached by a man who first seemed to be asking for directions. When Walter turned toward him, the man shoved him hard, grabbed at him, and struck him during the struggle before taking what he could and running. Walter remembers the shock more than anything: how ordinary the stop had seemed seconds before, how quickly it turned into helplessness, and how exposed he felt standing beside his truck in a place he had visited countless times for work. What has stayed with him most is not only that he was attacked, but that he had not seen it coming and did not know what to do quickly enough to stop it.

In the weeks afterward, Walter found himself dwelling on what the assault meant. He had come to believe that the basic rules he had lived by—that if you worked hard, kept your word, and treated people decently, the world was mostly understandable—no longer held. He said it felt as if his old beliefs about how life works had been “completely destroyed.” Just as painful was the way he judged himself. He was certain he should have handled it differently, should have read the situation sooner, should have done something more effective in the moment. Since then, he has struggled to trust his own judgment, saying in different ways that he cannot trust himself to do the right thing when it matters. The thought that frightened him most was that if he let himself really think about the assault, he would not be able to handle where his mind would go.

Those beliefs have shaped the way he gets through his days. Because he is convinced that thinking about the event will overwhelm him, Walter works hard to stay busy and keep his mind occupied. He picks up extra delivery tasks when he can, lingers over errands, and fills quiet stretches with little jobs so there is less room for his mind to wander back to the assault. The same fear drives how forcefully he pushes the memory away; when details begin to surface, he tries hard not to think about them at all, cutting himself off mid-thought and turning immediately to something practical. His self-doubt also feeds this pattern. Not trusting himself to cope, he relies on constant activity rather than reflection, as if stillness itself were dangerous. At home, especially in the evenings when there is less structure, he often overeats to blunt the distress and to give himself something immediate and absorbing to do.

This has become most visible in the setting of his work. As a delivery driver, he spends much of the day moving from stop to stop, and the truck has become both refuge and trap. He tells himself that if he just keeps to the route, keeps unloading, keeps scanning invoices and addresses, he can get through the day without his mind catching up with him. On days when there is downtime between deliveries, he notices the assault crowding closer in his thoughts, and he responds by inventing reasons to stay in motion or by eating heavily when he gets the chance. The strategy makes sense to him in the moment: if he stops, he fears he will come apart. But over months, his world has narrowed around this effort not to think.

His wife has noticed that he is physically present but mentally elsewhere, always occupied, reluctant to sit quietly, quick to shut down any conversation that comes near what happened. Walter does not describe this as healing. Rather, he speaks as a man trying to hold shut a door he no longer trusts himself to open safely. By the time he sought help, he was worn down by the effort of managing himself this way every day. He came in because he could see that the assault was still governing his life—through the busyness, the forced pushing away of thoughts, the overeating—and because he is afraid that if he cannot find another way to live with what happened, he will spend the rest of his life feeling unsafe in the world and unable to trust his own mind.
